section_title: What if we think we need nothing, but Christ sees our need?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 14 To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. 15 I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot. How I wish you were one or the other! 16 So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!

17 You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. 18 I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich, white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed, and salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see. 19 Those I love I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent.

20 Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me. 21 To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne. 22 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

context_lines: Laodicea receives a searching correction from Jesus, the faithful and true Witness and the Originator of God’s creation. His truthful assessment stands against the church’s confidence that it is wealthy and needs nothing.

The picture of lukewarmness expresses His rejection of its present condition. He describes a community that does not recognize its own poverty, blindness and nakedness. Its own account of success has left it unable to see what He sees.

The remedies come from Him: refined gold, white clothing and salve for the eyes. These pictures answer the needs He has just named. He then explains that His rebuke and discipline come from love, and calls for earnest repentance. The warning is severe, but the invitation remains open.

Jesus stands at the door and knocks, offering a shared meal to the person who hears and opens. The letter is addressed to a church and reaches each hearer within it. It closes with the promise of sharing His throne, just as He overcame and sat down with His Father. The final appeal again asks everyone able to hear to listen to the Spirit’s message.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/3.htm) understand lukewarmness as a complacent profession of faith lacking warmth and commitment. They explain the preference for cold or hot comparatively: open indifference is more readily recognized than self-satisfied religion. Gill nevertheless allows that members possess spiritual life while lacking fervor. The description does not produce a unanimous conclusion about every member’s salvation.

The clothing and meal receive different emphases. Wesley explains the white garments as true holiness and the supper as Christ sharing His grace now and life with Him eternally. Gill favors Christ’s righteousness as the clothing and reads the supper especially in connection with His return and the kingdom. Both direct the hearer toward receiving from Christ what self-sufficiency cannot supply.

Wesley and Gill also understand Jesus as the source and author of creation. The Greek arche can mean beginning, origin or rule; [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/746.htm) places Revelation 3:14 under origin or active cause. That supports the BSB’s wording, Originator. The same connection with creation through the Word appears in [John 1:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/1.htm).
god_plan_lines: The purpose of loving discipline appears elsewhere in Scripture. [Hebrews 12:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/12.htm) describes God correcting His children for their good, so they may share His holiness. Laodicea’s correction belongs within that larger pattern of love calling people away from a destructive course.

The meal and throne also recall Jesus’ promise to His disciples in [Luke 22:28–30](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/22.htm): sharing His table and kingdom after standing with Him through trials. This is a scriptural parallel, not a claim that the two passages describe every detail in the same way. Christ’s purpose reaches beyond exposing the church’s failure to bringing those who respond into fellowship with Him and participation in His victory.
